subject: multilevel testlet Rasch model variance estimates off

messages.author: 7fffd6a458b15b54
messages.subject: multilevel testlet Rasch model variance estimates off
parts:
Hi Bob,

I am trying to using Stan to estimate a multilevel testlet Rasch model: there are 36 items that belong to 6 testlets, and there are also 100 teacher and every 20 students are nested within 1 teacher.
I used the attached Stan code for estimation, but the estimates for the variance estimates are really off (the generating sd values are 1 while the estimates are about 0.1).
Would it be possible for you to take a look the Stan codes and output to see whether something is wrong? 

Thanks in advance for your help.
Yong

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] multilevel testlet Rasch model variance estimates off
parts:
Is there a reason you're using such a non-standard parameterization
here? That wasn't a rhetorical question, I just don't understand
the parameterization as it's so unfamiliar (but then I'm hardly an
expert on IRT models!).

I'd suspect you have too many degrees of freedom from all
the scale parameters. I just wrote a chapter on problematic posteriors that
discusses how to pin down IRT (i.e., Rasch) parameters, though that
assumed you had a discrimination parameter per test item. I'd also
recommend Gelman and Hill's regression book, which has several sections
in IRT models, including hierarchical variants.

I would also strongly encourage you to use vectors for this kind
of coding, because all the hard-coded indices are hard to read and
error prone.

testlet1 ~ normal(0,1);
testlet2 ~ normal(0,1);
testlet3 ~ normal(0,1);
testlet4 ~ normal(0,1);
testlet5 ~ normal(0,1);
testlet6 ~ normal(0,1);
sigma_theta ~ cauchy(0,5);
sigma_teacher ~ cauchy(0,5);
sigma_testlet1 ~ cauchy(0,5);
sigma_testlet2 ~ cauchy(0,5);
sigma_testlet3 ~ cauchy(0,5);
sigma_testlet4 ~ cauchy(0,5);
sigma_testlet5 ~ cauchy(0,5);
sigma_testlet6 ~ cauchy(0,5);

for(k in 1:6)
y[k] ~ bernoulli_logit(mu_theta*ones+sigma_theta*theta+sigma_teacher*teacher_trans+sigma_testlet1*testlet1 -
beta[k] * ones);
for(k in 7:12)
y[k] ~ bernoulli_logit(mu_theta*ones+sigma_theta*theta+sigma_teacher*teacher_trans+sigma_testlet2*testlet2 -
beta[k] * ones);
for(k in 13:18)
y[k] ~ bernoulli_logit(mu_theta*ones+sigma_theta*theta+sigma_teacher*teacher_trans+sigma_testlet3*testlet3 -
beta[k] * ones);
for(k in 19:24)
y[k] ~ bernoulli_logit(mu_theta*ones+sigma_theta*theta+sigma_teacher*teacher_trans+sigma_testlet4*testlet4 -
beta[k] * ones);
for(k in 25:30)
y[k] ~ bernoulli_logit(mu_theta*ones+sigma_theta*theta+sigma_teacher*teacher_trans+sigma_testlet5*testlet5 -
beta[k] * ones);
for(k in 31:36)
y[k] ~ bernoulli_logit(mu_theta*ones+sigma_theta*theta+sigma_teacher*teacher_trans+sigma_testlet6*testlet6 -
beta[k] * ones);
}

Declare

matrix[n_item,n_student,6] y;

vector[6] testlet;
vector<lower=0>[6] sigma_testlet;

and then you can write the model as:

testlet ~ normal(0,1);
sigma_testlet ~ cauchy(0,5);

for (k1 in 1:6) {
real y_hat;
y_hat <- mu_theta
+ sigma_theta * theta
+ sigma_teacher * teacher_trans
+ sigma_testlet[k1] * testlet[k1];
for (k2 in 1:6)
y[k1,k2] ~ bernoulli_logit(y_hat);
}

So I'd think you'd want something more like:

y_hat <- mu_theta + theta + teacher_trans + testlet[k1]

without any of the sigma or maybe just one of them. It's unusual
to use an intercept mu_theta, as you only care about the difference between the
difficulty and ability parameters. Usually the difficulty is
negated.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] multilevel testlet Rasch model variance estimates off
parts:
Have you tried just the literal translation of the WinBUGS
model into Stan? I'd do that and make sure it's fitting
first before trying to optimize. Is this still for
the 3PL model?

Then I'd suggest

y[i,j] ~ bernoulli(c[i] + (1 - c[i]) * inv_logit(a[i] * (theta[j] - b[i])));

where c[i] is random chance, a[i] is discrimination, theta[j] is ability and
b[i] is difficulty.

This model is tricky because you can rescale a, theta, and b and get
the same predictions, and also translate theta and b and get the same
answer. So to get good mixing, you have to do something to fix the scale
so not all of a, theta and b can vary, and also to fix the location of
theta or b.

We've fit the 2PL model no problem, so I'm not imagining 3PL is that big
of a jump, though it does introduce another degree of freedom in allowing
an alternative explanation for lots of students getting a problem right.

- Bob

> estimated using Winbugs, although it took more than 10 hours for the model to converge.

{

for (i in 1:I) {
                     r[j,i]<-response[j,i]
}
}

for (j in 1:J) {
for (i in 1:6) {
                p[j,i] <-1/(1+exp(-(theta[j]+thetat[class[j]]+testlet1[j]-b[i])))

       tau1 ~ dgamma(1,1)
tau2 ~ dgamma(1,1)
tau3 ~ dgamma(1,1)
tau4 ~ dgamma(1,1)
tau5 ~ dgamma(1,1)
tau6 ~ dgamma(1,1)          
var[1] <- 1/tau1
var[2] <- 1/tau2
var[3] <- 1/tau3
  var[4] <- 1/tau4
       var[5] <- 1/tau5
var[6] <- 1/tau6
               
for (t in 1:T) {
thetat[t] ~ dnorm(0, taut)
}



# Variance of Ability at the teacher-Level
taut ~ dgamma(1,1)
vart<- 1 / taut       
               

## Item Difficulty
 for (i in 1:I-1) {

OK --- I forgot the body of the first e-mail.

I meant literally translate the model distribution for
distribution. Then when it's working start tweaking it.

Do keep in mind that Stan uses sd to parameterize normal,
not precision, so what looks like this in WinBUGs:

u ~ dnorm(v,w);

needs to be:

u ~ normal(v, 1 / sqrt(w));

in Stan.


The first thing I'd do once it's working is replace pairs
like this

u <- 1/(1 + exp(-v))
w ~ dbern(u)

with the simpler

w ~ bernoulli_logit(v);

But to start, I'd just literally try copying it line for line first and
then gradually clean it up bit-by-bit once it's working.

- Bob

> On Mon, Feb 17, 2014 at 7:42 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
>
> Have you tried just the literal translation of the WinBUGS
> model into Stan? I'd do that and make sure it's fitting
> first before trying to optimize. Is this still for
> the 3PL model?
>
> Then I'd suggest
>
> y[i,j] ~ bernoulli(c[i] + (1 - c[i]) * inv_logit(a[i] * (theta[j] - b[i])));
>
> where c[i] is random chance, a[i] is discrimination, theta[j] is ability and
> b[i] is difficulty.
>
> This model is tricky because you can rescale a, theta, and b and get
> the same predictions, and also translate theta and b and get the same
> answer. So to get good mixing, you have to do something to fix the scale
> so not all of a, theta and b can vary, and also to fix the location of
> theta or b.
>
> We've fit the 2PL model no problem, so I'm not imagining 3PL is that big
> of a jump, though it does introduce another degree of freedom in allowing
> an alternative explanation for lots of students getting a problem right.
>
